acts.title: Text A · A thread with half the words missing
text: Read this the way you would read it on a phone: fast, and filling in the gaps without noticing that you are doing it.
[09:04] Morning. Any news on the Almaty contract?
[09:06] Not yet. Chased twice. Will chase again after lunch. Their office is bilingual, so the delay might be translation.
[09:07] Thanks. Meeting at eleven still on?
[09:11] Sorry — overran. Can’t make eleven. Twelve any good?
[09:12] Twelve fine. Room 3?
[09:12] Booked. Bring the figures?
[09:14] Which ones — March or the full year?
[09:15] Full year. March ones are wrong anyway. Misread the column headings, apparently.
[09:15] Knew it. Will do.
[09:16] One more thing. Semi-retired consultant coming Thursday. Not sure why. No idea what he wants.
[09:17] Ask Marat. He booked him.
[09:19] Did. Says it’s the bicentenary thing. Still none the wiser.
[09:20] Nor me. See you at twelve.

items.q: What are the two people arranging?
o: A meeting, moved from eleven to twelve

items.q: “Sorry — overran.” What has been left out?
o: I am sorry, but my previous meeting overran
I am sorry that you overran

acts.title: Text B · The note on the door
text: Back at 2. Key with Aigul next door — knock twice, she’s semi-retired so usually in. If not, try the flat below.
Parcel came. Left it inside on the table. Multicoloured one is yours, plain one isn’t — belongs to the office upstairs, so don’t open it. They’ll collect.
Boiler man rang. Says it’s illegal to leave it as it is, so he’s coming Thursday, not Tuesday. Rescheduled — sorry, nothing I could do about that.
Chairs for tonight: put them in a semicircle, not rows. Ten should be enough. Twelve if the interconnecting door is open.
If the bicentenary people ring again: no idea. Ask Marat. He’s the one who said yes.
Bread in the tin. Not the shelf. Long story, will explain later.
Back at 2. Probably.

items.s: The key is with a neighbour called Aigul.
Both parcels belong to the reader.
The boiler engineer has changed the day of his visit.
The writer knows the answer to the bicentenary question.
The bread is on the shelf.

items.q: What kind of word is left out most often in these notes?
o: The subject pronoun and the auxiliary

acts.title: Prefixes, and the words they build
rule: A prefix goes on the front of a word and changes its meaning in a predictable way. Learning nine prefixes is worth more than learning ninety words, because the prefix lets you read a word you have never seen before and be right about it.
points: il- before l, im- before m and p, ir- before r, in- elsewhere. illegal, impolite, irresponsible, inconvenient.
dis- reverses: disapprove, disagree. mis- means wrongly: misunderstand, misjudge, misspell.
bi- = two, mono- = one, semi- = half, multi- = many.
The prefix does not change the root. mis + spell = misspell, with two s. dis + satisfied = dissatisfied.
eg: il- before a word starting with l.
acts.careful: Biannual means twice a year; biennial means every two years. They look almost identical and mean opposite things, so if the difference matters, write it out in words instead.

write.q: Write two versions of the same message: first as a short note with as many words left out as possible, then as a full, formal email to somebody senior. The content is the same both times — you cannot attend tomorrow’s meeting, you have chased a supplier twice with no answer, and you want the meeting moved to Friday.
plan: note: leave out subjects and auxiliaries
write.model:
NOTE:
Can’t make tomorrow — sorry. Chased the supplier twice, nothing back. Friday any good? Will book Room 3 if so.

EMAIL:
Dear Ms Karimova,

I am afraid I will not be able to attend tomorrow’s meeting, and I apologize for the short notice.

I have chased the supplier twice and have still received no reply. I did not want us to meet without that information, since it is the only item on the agenda that cannot be decided without it.

Would it be possible to move the meeting to Friday? I am available all day, and I will book Room 3 as soon as you confirm.

Apologies again for the inconvenience.

Best regards,
Tilek
